title: Notes to Financial Statements & Disclosures
description: Determine appropriate financial statement disclosures and understand information presented in the notes.
html:
Why financial statement notes matter

The numbers presented on the face of the financial statements often do not provide enough information by themselves.

Notes to the financial statements provide additional information needed to understand the entity's financial position, financial performance and significant risks.

CPA mindset

A FAR question may ask:

  1. Should the item be recognized?
  2. Where should it be presented?
  3. Is additional disclosure required?
  4. Is disclosure alone sufficient?

Notes do not replace recognition

If U.S. GAAP requires an amount to be recognized in the financial statements, a company generally cannot avoid recognition merely by describing the item in a footnote.

Important principle

Required recognition cannot normally be replaced by disclosure.

Example

Assume a company has incurred $50,000 of wages before year-end that have not yet been paid.

If the wages meet the requirements for recognition, simply mentioning the unpaid wages in a note is not enough.

Significant accounting policies

Financial statement users need to understand the important accounting principles and methods used in preparing the statements.

Significant accounting policy information may include matters such as:

  • Revenue recognition policies
  • Inventory accounting methods
  • Depreciation and amortization methods
  • Basis of consolidation
  • Significant measurement policies

CPA trap

The purpose of an accounting-policy note is not to repeat every accounting rule contained in U.S. GAAP.

The disclosure should help users understand the significant policies relevant to the entity's financial statements.

Estimates and uncertainty

Financial reporting frequently requires estimates.

Examples include estimates involving:

  • Credit losses
  • Useful lives and residual values
  • Impairment
  • Contingencies
  • Fair value measurements
  • Certain income tax amounts

Depending on the facts and applicable guidance, disclosures may help users understand significant assumptions, uncertainty and exposure to changes in estimates.

Debt disclosures

A balance sheet may show a single debt amount, but users may also need information concerning the nature and terms of the borrowing.

Relevant information can include

  • Interest rates
  • Maturity dates
  • Collateral
  • Restrictive covenants
  • Future maturities
  • Defaults or other significant matters, when applicable

The balance sheet reports:

Long-Term Debt = $800,000

That amount alone may not explain when the debt matures, what interest rate applies, or whether assets are pledged as collateral.

Appropriate note disclosure supplies additional relevant information.

Contingencies

Contingencies are a major example of why recognition and disclosure must be considered separately.

Depending on the probability of loss, estimability and applicable guidance, a contingency may require:

  • Recognition and disclosure
  • Disclosure without recognition
  • Or, in some circumstances, neither recognition nor disclosure

CPA habit

Do not memorize: "lawsuit = disclose."

Analyze the probability, ability to estimate the loss, and the applicable rule.

Related-party disclosures

Transactions with related parties may require disclosure because they may not have occurred under the same conditions as transactions between independent parties.

Information may include

  • Nature of the relationship
  • Description of transactions
  • Dollar amounts of transactions
  • Amounts due to or from related parties

CPA trap

A transaction with a related party is not automatically fraudulent or invalid.

The issue is that users may need enough information to understand the relationship and transaction.

Commitments

Some contractual commitments may not yet create recognized assets or liabilities, but may still be important to financial statement users.

Applicable guidance may therefore require disclosure of significant commitments.

Example

A company signs a significant future purchase commitment.

If the agreement does not yet meet the requirements for recognizing an asset or liability, this does not automatically mean the commitment is irrelevant to financial statement users.

Subsequent events

Events occurring after the balance-sheet date but before the financial statements are issued or available to be issued can affect reporting.

Depending on the nature of the event, it may require adjustment, disclosure, or neither.

We will study the detailed rules separately in Lesson 9.

Concentrations and risks

Certain concentrations and significant risks may require disclosure when they create important exposure for the entity.

Examples can involve dependence on significant:

  • Customers
  • Suppliers
  • Markets
  • Products
  • Geographic areas

Face of statements versus notes

Face of Statements

Presents recognized financial statement amounts and required line items.

Notes

Explain, disaggregate and provide additional information needed to understand those statements.

CPA-style presentation example

Assume a company has:

Notes Payable $600,000
Current Portion $100,000
Long-Term Portion $500,000

The balance sheet may separately present the current and noncurrent portions.

The notes can then provide additional information about maturity dates, interest rates, collateral and other significant terms.

Big idea

Presentation answers: "What amount appears where?"

Disclosure answers: "What additional information does the user need to understand that amount?"

What you should know after this lesson

  • Understand the purpose of financial statement notes.
  • Know that disclosure does not normally replace required recognition.
  • Understand significant accounting policy disclosures.
  • Recognize why estimates and uncertainty may require additional information.
  • Understand the purpose of debt, contingency, related-party and commitment disclosures.
  • Distinguish information presented on the face of statements from information explained in the notes.

quiz.prompt: A company has incurred $70,000 of employee compensation before year-end that meets the requirements for recognition, but the amount will not be paid until next year. Which treatment is most appropriate?

choices.text: Disclose the obligation only in the notes and record nothing
Wait until cash is paid because financial statements report only cash transactions
Record the amount directly as a reduction of common stock
Recognize the expense and liability; disclosure does not substitute for required recognition

quiz.explanation: When an expense and related liability meet the requirements for recognition, the company records them in the financial statements. A note cannot normally be used as a substitute for required recognition.
